text: A users table can be keyed on the email address, or on a generated integer or UUID. Argue for one of these as the primary key of a production system, and explain precisely what breaks in the design you rejected when a user changes their email address.

expected_concepts.hint: a generated key carries no business meaning and therefore never has to change
email is data about the user, and user data changes
a primary key must be immutable for the lifetime of the row
every foreign key referencing the old value must be updated in the same transaction

common_misconceptions: argues email is fine because a UNIQUE constraint already prevents duplicates
believes ON UPDATE CASCADE makes a mutable primary key free of consequences
reference_answer: Use a surrogate key - a bigint identity or a UUID - and put a UNIQUE constraint on the email. The reason is that a primary key is an identity, and identity must be immutable: it is copied into every referencing table, into caches, into logs, into URLs and into other systems' records. Email is business data, and business data changes. If email were the key, a single address change would have to rewrite every foreign key in every child table atomically. ON UPDATE CASCADE can do that inside one database, but it rewrites and re-indexes an unbounded number of rows in one transaction, and it cannot reach anything outside the database - a cached row, an analytics warehouse, a partner's record. Uniqueness is a separate concern that a UNIQUE constraint handles, and a citext or normalised column handles case. The tradeoffs worth naming: a surrogate key adds a join to reach the human-readable value, and the choice between bigint and UUID is itself a real one - bigint is narrower and clusters well in a B-tree, random UUIDs scatter inserts across the index and inflate every referencing row, which is why UUIDv7 or ULID exists.
follow_up_seeds: When is a natural composite key the better choice?

text: Students enrol in courses, and each enrolment carries a grade and an enrolment date. Show the tables, primary keys and foreign keys you would create, and explain why the grade cannot sensibly live on either the students table or the courses table.

expected_concepts.hint: neither side can hold a single reference to the other
an enrolments table whose rows are the relationship instances
(student_id, course_id) as the key, or a surrogate key plus a unique constraint
grade is a property of the pairing, not of either entity

common_misconceptions: adds a grade column to students, silently assuming one course per student
stores a comma-separated list of course ids on the student row
reference_answer: Three tables. students(id PK, ...), courses(id PK, ...), and enrolments(student_id FK -> students.id, course_id FK -> courses.id, grade, enrolled_on) with primary key (student_id, course_id) - or a surrogate id plus a UNIQUE (student_id, course_id) if the enrolment itself must be referenced from elsewhere. The grade cannot live on students because a student has one grade per course, not one grade; it cannot live on courses for the mirror-image reason. It is an attribute of the relationship instance, and a junction table is what gives that instance somewhere to exist. This is the general rule for many-to-many: a foreign key column can express 'many rows point at one row', so it handles one-to-many in either direction, but many-to-many needs a third table. The composite key also enforces the business rule that a student enrols in a course at most once, and the same (student_id, course_id) index serves lookups by student; add an index on course_id for the other direction, since a composite index cannot be used for a filter on its second column alone.

text: An orders table stores customer_id, customer_name and customer_city on every row. Name the anomalies this produces on insert, update and delete, say which normal form it violates and why, and show the corrected tables.

expected_concepts.hint: a renamed customer must be rewritten on every one of their order rows
customer_name depends on customer_id, which is not the key of orders
non-key attributes must depend on the key, not on another non-key attribute
split into customers and orders, joined on customer_id

common_misconceptions: identifies the redundancy but cannot name which dependency causes it
asserts normalisation is always correct without acknowledging the read cost
reference_answer: The table violates third normal form. Its key is order_id, but customer_name and customer_city depend on customer_id, which is itself a non-key attribute - a transitive dependency order_id -> customer_id -> customer_name. Three anomalies follow. Update: renaming a customer requires rewriting every order row they have, and a partial update leaves two spellings of the same customer in the table with no way to tell which is right. Insert: a customer who has not yet ordered cannot be recorded at all, because there is no order row to hang them on. Delete: removing a customer's last order destroys the only copy of their name and city. The fix is to decompose into customers(id PK, name, city) and orders(id PK, customer_id FK -> customers.id, ...), recovering the original view with a join. Each fact is then stored exactly once, which is what normalisation is for. Worth adding that the decomposition is lossless and dependency-preserving, and that the cost is a join on the read path - a cost that is usually right to pay, and that section on denormalisation exists to revisit deliberately rather than by accident.

text: A reporting endpoint joins five normalised tables and has become too slow. The team proposes storing a denormalised copy of the joined result. Explain what you gain, which guarantee you give up, and the mechanisms available for keeping the denormalised copy correct.

expected_concepts.hint: read cost falls, write cost and correctness risk rise
the copy can disagree with its source, and nothing in the schema prevents it
let the database own the derivation and the refresh
decide explicitly how out of date the report may be

common_misconceptions: denormalises before establishing that the join is actually the bottleneck
maintains the copy with application code in a separate transaction from the write
reference_answer: The gain is a read that touches one table instead of five, removing join and planner work from the hot path. What you give up is single-source-of-truth: the copy is derived data, and derived data drifts. Nothing in the schema prevents the copy from disagreeing with the tables it came from, so correctness moves from a database constraint into human discipline, which is the real cost. Mechanisms, roughly in order of safety: a materialised view, where the database owns the definition and the refresh, so the derivation cannot be forgotten and REFRESH CONCURRENTLY keeps reads available; triggers, which update the copy in the same transaction as the write, correct but adding write latency and lock footprint; an asynchronous job or CDC consumer, which decouples the write path at the price of a bounded staleness window; and application-level dual writes, which are the most common and the most error-prone, because every future write path must remember. Before any of this, confirm with EXPLAIN ANALYZE that the join is the bottleneck rather than a missing index or a bad cardinality estimate, and decide the tolerable staleness explicitly - a report that may be five minutes old is a much cheaper system than one that may not.
follow_up_seeds: How would you detect that the denormalised copy has drifted?

text: Explain the difference between an INNER JOIN and a LEFT JOIN. Then explain why putting a condition on the right-hand table in the WHERE clause of a LEFT JOIN usually turns it back into an inner join, and where that condition belongs instead.

expected_concepts.hint: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched left rows, padding the right columns with NULL
a comparison against NULL is UNKNOWN, so the padded rows fail the filter
conditions on the right table belong in ON; conditions on the left in WHERE
missing rows in a report are the usual symptom

common_misconceptions: believes ON and WHERE are interchangeable for outer joins
expects NULL = 'x' to evaluate to false rather than UNKNOWN
reference_answer: An INNER JOIN emits only pairs of rows that satisfy the join condition. A LEFT JOIN emits those, plus every left row that matched nothing, with the right table's columns filled with NULL. The order of evaluation is what causes the trap: the join runs first and produces the NULL-padded rows, then the WHERE clause filters that result. A predicate such as WHERE o.status = 'paid' is UNKNOWN for a NULL-padded row - in three-valued logic a comparison with NULL is neither true nor false - and WHERE keeps only rows where the predicate is true, so exactly the rows the LEFT JOIN was written to preserve are discarded, silently reproducing an inner join. The fix is to move the condition into the ON clause: LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid' restricts which right rows are eligible to match while still keeping unmatched left rows. The rule of thumb is that a filter on the outer-joined table belongs in ON, and a filter on the preserved table belongs in WHERE. The deliberate exception is WHERE o.id IS NULL, which is the idiom for finding left rows with no match at all.

text: Name the three join algorithms a relational planner typically chooses between, describe the input shape each one suits, and explain what information the planner uses to decide. Why might it pick a hash join for a query that has an index on the join column?

expected_concepts.hint: good when the outer side is tiny and the inner side is indexed
build a hash table on the smaller side, probe with the larger; equality only
both inputs sorted on the join key, then a single co-ordinated pass
estimated row counts and distributions from the statistics tables
the plan with the lowest estimated cost wins, not the one using the most indexes

common_misconceptions: assumes an available index always makes an index nested loop the best plan
believes the planner chooses by rules rather than by estimated cost
reference_answer: Nested loop: for each row of the outer input, find matches in the inner input. It wins when the outer side yields very few rows and the inner side has an index on the join column, making each probe cheap; it degrades badly as the outer row count grows, because the cost is essentially outer_rows multiplied by the probe cost. Hash join: build an in-memory hash table on the smaller input, then stream the larger input through it. It handles equality joins of two large inputs in roughly linear time, needs no ordering and no index, and spills to disk if the build side exceeds working memory. Merge join: requires both inputs sorted on the join key, then walks them together in one pass; it is the winner when the sort is free because both sides arrive ordered from an index scan, and it emits its output already ordered on the join key, which a later ORDER BY, GROUP BY or merge can reuse for free. The planner chooses by estimated cost, computed from table statistics - row counts, column distributions, most-common values, null fraction - and index availability. It will pick a hash join over an indexed nested loop when it estimates the outer side returns many rows, because thousands of random index probes with their random I/O cost more than one sequential scan plus a hash build. When that choice looks wrong, the usual root cause is a stale or insufficiently detailed statistic, not the algorithm.
follow_up_seeds: What would you check first when the planner's row estimate is far off?

text: Explain, in terms of what the database actually does at read time, why a B-tree index on a column makes lookups on that column faster. Then describe the cost the same index imposes on INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, and why indexing every column is a bad default.

expected_concepts.hint: an ordered structure with a shallow height, so a lookup is a few page reads
descend the tree to the key instead of scanning every page of the table
every index must be updated in the same transaction as the row
indexes occupy disk and compete for the same buffer cache as the table

common_misconceptions: believes an index speeds up all queries on the table rather than those on its columns
treats indexes as free because they are invisible to the application
reference_answer: Without an index the database must read every page of the table and test each row - a sequential scan, costing time proportional to the table size. A B-tree stores the column's values in sorted order in a shallow, high-fanout tree, so finding a value means descending three or four levels, each a single page read, and then following a pointer to the row: logarithmic rather than linear, and typically a handful of I/Os regardless of table size. The same ordering also serves range scans, ORDER BY and prefix matching, which is why B-trees rather than hash indexes are the default. The cost falls on writes. Every INSERT must also insert into every index on the table, and may split a page; every DELETE must remove those entries; an UPDATE that changes an indexed column is an index delete plus insert. So a table with eight indexes does roughly nine structures' worth of work per write, in the same transaction, holding locks the whole time. Indexes also consume disk and, more importantly, buffer cache that the table's own pages need. Hence the default: index for the queries you actually run, drop indexes nothing uses, and remember that an index on a low-selectivity column may not even be chosen once created.
follow_up_seeds: How would you find indexes in production that nothing is using?

text: A table has a single index on (tenant_id, created_at). Which of these can use it efficiently and which cannot: a filter on tenant_id alone; a filter on created_at alone; a filter on tenant_id with a range scan on created_at? Explain the rule that decides, and what changes if you reverse the column order.

expected_concepts.hint: the index is sorted by the first column, then by the second within it
a query can use any leading prefix of the index columns
equality columns first, the range column last
once a range is opened on a column, later columns are no longer ordered usefully

common_misconceptions: believes a composite index works as if it were two separate single-column indexes
puts the range column first, which prevents the equality column from narrowing the scan
reference_answer: A composite index is sorted by tenant_id, and within each tenant_id by created_at - like a phone book ordered by surname then first name. Filtering on tenant_id alone uses it well: all matching entries are contiguous. Filtering on tenant_id plus a range on created_at is the ideal case: the equality picks a contiguous block and the range picks a contiguous slice inside it, so the scan reads exactly the rows wanted. Filtering on created_at alone cannot use the index for a seek, because entries for a given date are scattered across every tenant's section - just as a phone book cannot find everyone called Priya. A planner may still choose a full index scan if the index is much narrower than the table, but that is a scan, not a seek, and the cost is linear. The rule is the leftmost prefix: a query can use a leading prefix of the index columns, and only the first non-equality predicate can be a range - columns after it are not usefully ordered. Reversing to (created_at, tenant_id) would serve created_at-only queries and cross-tenant time ranges, but the important tenant-plus-time query would then have to scan the whole time range and discard other tenants' rows. For a multi-tenant system the given order is right.
follow_up_seeds: When would you add a third column purely to make the index covering?

text: A query filters on a column that has an index, but EXPLAIN shows a sequential scan. Give three distinct reasons a planner can legitimately ignore an available index, and for each say how you would confirm it is the reason in this case.

expected_concepts.hint: a predicate matching a large fraction of rows makes a scan cheaper
wrapping the column in a function or casting it hides the indexed value
stale statistics produce a row estimate that justifies the wrong plan
compare estimated with actual rows, and test the hypothesis by changing one thing

common_misconceptions: concludes the planner is broken and reaches for a hint or a forced index
assumes any query mentioning an indexed column is able to use the index
reference_answer: First, low selectivity: if the predicate matches a large fraction of the table - roughly more than five to ten percent - an index scan means many random single-page reads plus heap lookups, which costs more than reading the table sequentially, so the planner is right. Confirm by running the predicate as a COUNT and comparing it with the table's row count, and by checking whether the estimated row count in EXPLAIN is large. Second, a non-sargable predicate: WHERE lower(email) = ... , WHERE created_at::date = ... , or a comparison whose types force an implicit cast, all ask for a value the index does not store. Confirm by rewriting the predicate to compare the bare column, for example a half-open timestamp range instead of a cast to date, and re-running EXPLAIN; the fix is that rewrite or an expression index. Third, stale or missing statistics: the planner's estimate is far from reality, so it costs the wrong plan. Confirm by comparing the estimated and actual row counts in EXPLAIN ANALYZE - a large discrepancy is the signal - then run ANALYZE and retry. Other legitimate reasons worth mentioning are a very small table, where a scan is simply cheaper, and a partial index whose WHERE clause does not cover the query. Forcing the index without establishing the cause treats the symptom.

text: State what each letter of ACID guarantees. Then take a transfer of money between two accounts and explain precisely which of those guarantees prevents the money from being deducted from one account but never credited to the other when the process crashes midway.

expected_concepts.hint: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability, each a distinct promise
all statements in the transaction take effect or none do
an uncommitted transaction is rolled back when the database restarts
both statements must be inside one transaction for the guarantee to apply

common_misconceptions: attributes the guarantee to consistency or durability rather than to atomicity
assumes two separate statements are atomic without an explicit transaction
reference_answer: Atomicity: a transaction's statements all take effect or none do; there is no partial outcome. Consistency: a committed transaction moves the database from one state satisfying its declared constraints to another - it is about constraints such as foreign keys and CHECKs, not about application correctness in general. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not observe each other's intermediate states, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability: once commit returns, the effects survive a crash. The half-transfer is prevented by atomicity. With both the debit and the credit inside one transaction, a crash before commit leaves the transaction uncommitted, and recovery rolls it back using the write-ahead log, so neither statement is visible. Durability is a different promise - that a transfer which did commit is not lost - and consistency would only catch the half-transfer if a constraint happened to encode the invariant, which for a balance total it usually cannot. The practical caveat worth stating is that the guarantee depends on both statements actually being in one transaction: two auto-committed statements from the application are two transactions, and no ACID property spans them.
follow_up_seeds: What if the credit goes to a different service, not a second table?

text: A database reports a transaction as committed. Explain the mechanism that makes that promise survive an immediate power loss, why writing the modified data pages themselves is not what provides it, and what an operator gives up by turning synchronous commit off.

expected_concepts.hint: the change is logged and flushed before commit returns; pages are written later
commit means the log record is on stable storage, not that the table is updated
an OS write only reaches the page cache; fsync is what forces the device
asynchronous commit trades a bounded window of committed-but-lost transactions for throughput

common_misconceptions: believes commit flushes the modified table pages to disk
treats a successful write() call as durable without an fsync
reference_answer: Durability comes from write-ahead logging. Before any modified page may be written back, a log record describing the change is appended to the WAL, and at commit that log is flushed to stable storage with an fsync; only then does commit return. The table's own pages stay dirty in the buffer pool and are written later by a checkpointer. Writing the data pages at commit would be far slower - they are scattered across the file, so it is random I/O, whereas the WAL is a single sequential append that a disk handles at full speed. It would also be unsafe on its own, since a crash midway through writing a set of pages leaves a torn state with nothing recording the intent. On restart, recovery replays committed log records whose pages had not been flushed and rolls back uncommitted ones. The fsync matters because an ordinary write only reaches the operating system's page cache, which power loss discards. Disabling synchronous commit lets commit return once the record is in the WAL buffer, before the flush: throughput improves markedly, and the price is a bounded window - typically a fraction of a second - in which acknowledged transactions can be lost after a crash. Note that atomicity is unaffected; the database does not become corrupt, it just loses recent commits.
follow_up_seeds: When is asynchronous commit an acceptable setting for real workloads?

text: Compare READ COMMITTED with REPEATABLE READ. Give a concrete two-transaction interleaving that behaves differently under the two levels, name the anomaly involved, and say which level you would default to for a web application and why.

expected_concepts.hint: each statement sees a fresh snapshot of committed data
the whole transaction sees one snapshot taken at its first read
the same row read twice in one transaction returns different values
match the level to whether the transaction reasons across multiple reads

common_misconceptions: believes READ COMMITTED can return uncommitted data
assumes REPEATABLE READ prevents all write anomalies, including write skew
reference_answer: Interleaving: transaction A reads row X and gets 100. Transaction B updates X to 150 and commits. A reads X again. Under READ COMMITTED, every statement takes a new snapshot of committed data, so A's second read returns 150 - a non-repeatable read, and A has now computed with two different values of the same row. Under REPEATABLE READ, A's snapshot is fixed at its first read, so the second read still returns 100 and A sees a single consistent point in time. Neither level ever exposes uncommitted data; that is READ UNCOMMITTED, which PostgreSQL does not implement separately. The practical default for a web application is READ COMMITTED - it is PostgreSQL's default, it holds no read snapshot across statements so it produces less bloat and fewer conflicts, and typical request handlers do one logical operation. Escalate deliberately: a transaction that reads several rows and reasons across them, such as a report or a balance check followed by a write, wants REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE. The important caveat is that REPEATABLE READ can abort with a serialization failure, so any code using it must be safe to retry - and it still permits write skew, which only SERIALIZABLE prevents.
follow_up_seeds: What is a phantom read, and which level is the first to prevent it?

text: Two on-call engineers each run a transaction that checks at least one other engineer is still on duty and, seeing that, marks themselves off duty. Both transactions commit and nobody is on call. Name this anomaly, explain why snapshot isolation permits it, and describe what SERIALIZABLE does differently.

expected_concepts.hint: two transactions read an overlapping set, then write disjoint rows
each sees a pre-transaction snapshot; no write-write conflict is detected
SSI tracks read-write dependencies and aborts one transaction of a dangerous cycle
the invariant spans rows, so no single-row constraint can protect it

common_misconceptions: believes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the rows each transaction writes would prevent it
assumes REPEATABLE READ in PostgreSQL is sufficient because it prevents phantoms
reference_answer: This is write skew. Under snapshot isolation each transaction reads from its own snapshot, taken before the other's write was visible, so both see two engineers on duty and both predicates pass. They then write different rows - each updates only its own record - so there is no write-write conflict for first-updater-wins to catch, and both commit. The invariant 'at least one engineer on duty' spans rows, so no unique or check constraint on a single row can defend it. The general shape is: two transactions read an overlapping set, make a decision from it, and write disjoint rows, each invalidating the other's premise. SERIALIZABLE, implemented in PostgreSQL as serializable snapshot isolation, additionally tracks which reads each transaction performed and the read-write dependencies between concurrent transactions; when it detects the dangerous structure that could not arise in any serial order, it aborts one with a serialization failure, and the application retries. The cost is real - predicate tracking overhead and retry logic that must exist and must be correct - so the alternatives are worth naming: SELECT FOR UPDATE on the rows that were read rather than the rows written, or materialising the invariant into a single row that both transactions must update and therefore conflict on.
follow_up_seeds: Why does locking only the rows you write fail to prevent this?

text: Two requests read the same row, each adds 10 to the value they read, and each writes the result back. The row ends up 10 higher rather than 20. Name this problem, and describe two different ways to prevent it - one pessimistic and one optimistic - including the cost of each.

expected_concepts.hint: a read-modify-write cycle where the second write overwrites the first
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE holds a row lock so the second reader waits
version column in the WHERE clause; zero rows updated means retry
UPDATE ... SET n = n + 10 removes the read-modify-write entirely

common_misconceptions: believes wrapping the two statements in a transaction is by itself sufficient
adds a lock without considering the throughput cost on a hot row
reference_answer: This is a lost update: both transactions read the same value, compute from it, and the later write silently overwrites the earlier one. A transaction alone does not prevent it at READ COMMITTED - both reads are legal and both writes are legal. Pessimistic: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the row before reading it, which takes an exclusive row lock so the second transaction blocks until the first commits and then reads the updated value. It is simple and always correct, and it costs throughput - requests serialise on that row, and holding the lock across any slow work in the transaction turns it into a queue, with deadlock risk if lock order is inconsistent. Optimistic: keep a version column, read it with the row, and write UPDATE ... SET value = ..., version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If another transaction won, zero rows are affected and the application retries. No locks are held, so it scales well under low contention, and the costs are wasted work plus mandatory retry logic that must be present everywhere the row is written. Under high contention on one row, the retries make it worse than a lock. Best of all here, if the operation really is just an increment, write UPDATE ... SET n = n + 10, which the database performs atomically and which removes the read-modify-write cycle altogether.
follow_up_seeds: Which approach would you choose for a single very hot counter row?

text: Explain the conditions under which two transactions deadlock in a relational database, what the database does when it detects one, and the single most effective application-side change that prevents most deadlocks in practice.

expected_concepts.hint: each holds a lock the other needs, producing a cycle in the wait-for graph
the database finds the cycle and aborts one transaction as the victim
always acquire rows in a consistent global order, which makes a cycle impossible
shorter transactions holding fewer locks reduce the window in which a cycle can form

common_misconceptions: expects the database to hang rather than abort one of the transactions
treats a deadlock error as a database bug rather than a condition to retry
reference_answer: A deadlock needs a cycle in the wait-for graph: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and asks for row 2, while B holds row 2 and asks for row 1. Neither can proceed and neither will release, so waiting forever is the only alternative to intervention. The classic example is two code paths that update the same pair of rows in opposite orders, which is easy to create accidentally when the order comes from an unsorted collection or from user input. Databases run a periodic deadlock detector, find the cycle, and abort one transaction as the victim with a specific error - in PostgreSQL SQLSTATE 40P01 - releasing its locks so the other proceeds. The victim's work is rolled back entirely. The most effective prevention is consistent lock ordering: always acquire rows in the same deterministic order, for example ascending primary key, so no cycle can form. Sorting the ids before the loop that updates them is often a one-line fix for a recurring production deadlock. Supporting measures: keep transactions short and never hold locks across a network call or user think-time; take the most contended lock first; and treat the deadlock error as retryable, since even with good discipline lock upgrades and index-level locks can still produce one.
follow_up_seeds: How would you find the two statements involved after the fact?

text: In PostgreSQL, a long-running SELECT does not block a concurrent UPDATE of the same rows, and the UPDATE does not block the SELECT. Explain the mechanism that makes this possible, what each statement sees, and the operational cost this design creates that a purely locking database does not have.

expected_concepts.hint: an update writes a new row version rather than overwriting the old one
each statement sees the versions committed as of its snapshot
dead versions accumulate and cannot be reclaimed while an old snapshot needs them
autovacuum reclaims dead tuples; a long transaction holds back the horizon

common_misconceptions: believes readers take shared locks that writers must wait for
treats bloat as a disk-space issue only, ignoring the effect on scan and cache efficiency
reference_answer: The mechanism is multiversion concurrency control. An UPDATE does not overwrite the row; it writes a new version of it and marks the old version as deleted by the updating transaction, and each version carries the transaction ids that created and removed it. Every statement runs against a snapshot, and a version is visible to it if the creating transaction had committed as of that snapshot and the removing one had not. So the long SELECT continues to read the old versions and sees a consistent point in time, while the UPDATE creates new ones - readers never block writers and writers never block readers. Writers still block writers on the same row, which is a genuine conflict. The cost is that dead versions accumulate in the table and its indexes and must be reclaimed by autovacuum, which can only remove a version once no snapshot could still need it. A long-running transaction therefore pins the horizon and prevents reclamation across the whole database, and the table bloats: it occupies more disk, every sequential scan reads more pages, and dead tuples displace live ones in the buffer cache, so performance degrades even for queries unrelated to the update. This is why idle-in-transaction sessions are a well-known production hazard in PostgreSQL and why monitoring the oldest transaction age matters.
follow_up_seeds: Why is an idle-in-transaction connection more dangerous than a slow query?

text: You run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a slow query. Explain what the gap between the estimated row count and the actual row count on a plan node tells you, and what you would do about a node whose estimate is a hundred times too low.

expected_concepts.hint: read the node with the largest estimate-versus-actual gap, from the inside out
every plan choice above the node was costed on a wrong row count
ANALYZE refreshes them; correlated columns need extended statistics
fix the estimate first, and only then consider rewriting or indexing

common_misconceptions: reads only the total execution time and ignores the per-node estimates
adds an index before establishing why the planner chose the plan it did
reference_answer: The estimate is what the planner believed when it chose the plan; the actual is what happened. A large divergence means the plan was chosen on false information, so the problem is usually not the executor but the estimate - and errors compound upward, because a bad row count at a leaf makes every join method and join order decision above it wrong. Find the deepest node with the largest ratio, since that is the origin rather than a consequence. An estimate a hundred times too low typically leads the planner to pick a nested loop expecting a handful of rows and then execute millions of index probes, or to under-size a hash table so it spills. Causes and fixes, in order: stale statistics after a bulk load, fixed by ANALYZE; correlated predicates, since the planner multiplies selectivities assuming independence, so filtering on city and postcode together gives a wildly low estimate - fixed with CREATE STATISTICS on the column group; a skewed column needing a higher statistics target; or an expression or join condition the planner cannot estimate at all, where the answer is to rewrite it. Also note that EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query, so a destructive statement must be wrapped in a transaction that is rolled back, and that its instrumentation adds measurable overhead to timings.
follow_up_seeds: What would you check if the estimates are accurate but the node is still slow?

text: An API endpoint lists 50 orders and, for each, its customer's name; the logs show 51 queries per request. Name this pattern, explain why an ORM makes it so easy to produce, and give two fixes that act at different layers, with the tradeoff each one carries.

expected_concepts.hint: one query for the list, then one per row for the related record
attribute access on a relationship silently issues a query
collect the ids and fetch the related rows with a single IN query
a join returns duplicated parent columns; two queries avoid that but add a round trip

common_misconceptions: blames per-query execution time rather than the number of network round trips
assumes an eager join is always the right fix regardless of the relationship's cardinality
reference_answer: This is the N+1 query problem: one query returns the 50 orders, then accessing each order's customer triggers a further query, giving 51. The cost is dominated by round trips, not by the work inside the database - fifty queries that each take a millisecond still add fifty milliseconds of latency that scales with the page size, so it degrades exactly as the result set grows. ORMs produce it easily because lazy loading makes a database call look like an attribute access: order.customer.name is indistinguishable in the source from reading a field, so the query is invisible at the call site and appears only in the logs. Fix one, at the query layer: fetch the relationship eagerly - a JOIN in a single query, or the ORM's equivalent such as joinedload. It is one round trip, and the tradeoff is that a join duplicates the parent's columns across every child row, which is wasteful for one-to-many and can make the result far larger than necessary. Fix two, at the access-pattern layer: batch the second fetch - collect the distinct customer ids and issue one query with IN, then stitch the results in memory, which is what selectinload and DataLoader do. Two round trips instead of one, but no row duplication, so it is usually the better choice for collections. Whichever is chosen, the durable fix is detection: assert on query counts in tests, or log a warning above a threshold, because the next lazy attribute access will look just as innocent.

text: A read replica is added to take load off the primary, and users start reporting that a record they have just saved is missing when the page reloads. Explain the mechanism causing this, and describe two different ways to fix it without abandoning the replica.

expected_concepts.hint: the replica applies the write stream some time after the primary commits
the primary commits without waiting for the replica to acknowledge
a user must see their own write, even if others may see it later
route by recency of the user's last write, or wait for a log position

common_misconceptions: concludes the write failed rather than that the read went to a lagging replica
proposes synchronous replication without acknowledging its latency and availability cost
reference_answer: With asynchronous replication the primary commits and returns as soon as its own write-ahead log is durable, then streams the log to the replica, which applies it some milliseconds or seconds later. The write went to the primary and the subsequent read went to a replica that had not yet applied it, so the user does not see their own write. This is a read-your-writes violation, and it is a consistency problem, not a bug in the write path. Fix one, sticky reads: after a user writes, route that user's reads to the primary for a bounded window - a cookie or session flag holding a timestamp is enough. Simple and effective; the cost is that the primary takes back some read load, concentrated on the most active users. Fix two, monitor the replica's log position: capture the primary's log sequence number at commit, pass it along with the request, and either wait for the chosen replica to reach it or fall back to the primary. More precise and it keeps more reads on replicas, at the cost of plumbing the position through the application. A third option is synchronous replication, which removes the lag but makes every write wait for a replica acknowledgement and makes the primary's availability depend on the replica's - usually too high a price for this symptom. Whichever is chosen, lag should be monitored and alerted on, and reads that genuinely tolerate staleness - dashboards, search, analytics - should stay on the replica deliberately.

text: An events table has grown to two billion rows, and queries almost always filter by a time range. Explain how partitioning by time would help, distinguish partitioning from sharding, and describe what happens to a query that does not include the partition key.

expected_concepts.hint: one logical table split into physical child tables by a key range
the planner skips partitions that cannot contain matching rows
partitioning is within one database; sharding spreads data across machines
the key must appear in the common query predicate or pruning cannot happen

common_misconceptions: uses partitioning and sharding as synonyms
expects a query without the partition key to still be fast
reference_answer: Range-partition the table by the event timestamp, typically one partition per day or month. The whole table remains one logical relation, but each partition is a separate physical table with its own indexes. Two things improve. Queries filtering on a time range benefit from partition pruning: the planner can prove which partitions could contain matching rows and skips the rest, so a query over one day touches one partition and one small index rather than a two-billion-row B-tree. Maintenance improves more dramatically: dropping old data becomes DROP TABLE on a partition - near-instant and reclaiming space immediately - instead of a bulk DELETE that rewrites indexes and leaves bloat behind. Vacuum, index rebuilds and bulk loads all operate per partition. Partitioning is not sharding: partitions live in one database instance, sharing its CPU, memory and single point of failure, so partitioning solves manageability and scan volume but not write throughput or capacity limits. Sharding distributes data across independent instances and buys those, at the price of cross-shard queries, distributed transactions and rebalancing. A query without the partition key cannot be pruned: the planner must scan every partition, which is at best equivalent to the unpartitioned table and often slightly worse, because of per-partition planning overhead and because a global index across partitions is not generally available. That is why the partition key must be chosen from the actual query predicates, and why a secondary access pattern may need its own index on every partition.
